descriptor: The largest living cat, hunting alone through the forests and mangroves of the Indian subcontinent.

range.summary: Fragmented populations across India, Bangladesh, Nepal and Bhutan, from Himalayan foothills to the Sundarbans delta.

regions.name: Central India
regions.note: Central India's forests, from Kanha to Tadoba, form India's largest tiger landscape.

regions.name: Nepal Terai
regions.note: Nepal's Terai tigers rose from 121 in 2009 to 355 in 2022.

regions.name: Russian Far East
regions.note: Amur tigers fell to under 40 in the 1940s; Russia's Far East now holds over 500.

regions.name: Sumatra
regions.note: Sumatra holds the last island tigers, a Critically Endangered population.

regions.name: Bali
regions.note: The Bali tiger's last confirmed record was a tigress shot in west Bali in 1937.

regions.name: Java
regions.note: The Javan tiger's last confirmed sighting was in Meru Betiri National Park in 1976.

regions.name: Caspian range
regions.note: The Caspian tiger died out from Turkey to Central Asia; one of the last was killed in Turkey in 1970.

regions.name: South Korea
regions.note: South Korea's last known wild tiger was shot near Gyeongju in 1922.

regions.name: South China
regions.note: No wild South China tiger has been confirmed since the late 1980s; 2001-02 surveys found none.

regions.name: Cambodia
regions.note: Cambodia's last tiger was camera-trapped in Mondulkiri in 2007; it was declared functionally extinct in 2016.

regions.name: Sariska
regions.note: Poaching emptied Sariska of tigers by 2004; tigers from Ranthambore were moved back in from 2008.

regions.name: Panna
regions.note: Panna's last tiger vanished in late 2008; tigresses brought in from March 2009 rebuilt the population.

source.label: IUCN Red List: Panthera tigris (Goodrich et al. 2022)

rangeHistory.note: Covers the whole species, not only Bengal tigers; circles are approximate and extinct subspecies are shown as lost ranges.

source.label: NTCA, Status of Tigers in India 2022

population.note: The 1900 figure is a widely cited historical back-estimate, not a census. Counts before 2006 used pugmark methods and are not directly comparable with camera-trap estimates.

threats.title: Habitat loss and fragmentation
threats.detail: Roads, mines and farmland sever the corridors that connect reserves.

threats.title: Poaching
threats.detail: Demand for skins, bones and body parts persists across Asia.

threats.title: Prey depletion
threats.detail: Bushmeat hunting removes the deer and wild pigs tigers depend on.

threats.title: Conflict with people
threats.detail: Retaliatory killings follow livestock losses on reserve edges.

places.name: Ranthambore National Park
places.note: Dry deciduous forest with old fort ruins and high sighting rates.

places.name: Bandhavgarh National Park
places.note: One of the highest tiger densities in India.

places.name: Kanha National Park
places.note: Sal forest and meadows; the setting that inspired The Jungle Book.

places.name: Sundarbans
places.note: Mangrove tigers that swim between islands. Sightings are rare.

places.name: Chitwan National Park
places.note: Grassland and riverine forest at the foot of the Himalaya.

sightings.tip: Late dry season, March to May, draws tigers to the few remaining waterholes. Most Indian parks close core zones during the monsoon.

actions.title: Choose certified wood and paper
actions.detail: FSC-certified products reduce pressure on the forests tigers live in.

actions.title: Never buy tiger products
actions.detail: Skins, bone wine, teeth and claws fund the poaching networks.

actions.title: Travel with responsible operators
actions.detail: Pick lodges that fund patrols, employ locals and cap vehicle numbers.

actions.title: Fund rangers directly
actions.detail: Anti-poaching patrols are one of the most cost-effective interventions.
